clinicalPearls: One of the episodic syndromes that may be associated with migraine (ICHD-3), formerly grouped with the childhood periodic syndromes; most affected children have a strong family history of migraine or later develop migraine themselves
Presents in toddlers and preschool children (typically 2-4 years) with recurrent, sudden, brief attacks of vertigo and unsteadiness lasting minutes and resolving spontaneously
During an attack the child suddenly appears frightened, off-balance or refuses to walk, may clutch a parent and become pale, sweaty or nauseated; observable nystagmus supports the diagnosis
Consciousness is fully preserved with no ictal confusion or postictal drowsiness, which helps distinguish attacks from epileptic seizures
Attacks are stereotyped and self-limiting and the child is entirely well between episodes, with a normal neurological and audiological examination

Diagnosis is clinical using ICHD-3 criteria (at least five stereotyped attacks with spontaneous resolution and normal examination and investigations between attacks); routine investigation is not needed in typical cases
The condition remits spontaneously over months to a few years and is often followed by more typical migraine headaches later in childhood or adolescence
Reassurance is the mainstay of management; migraine-preventive strategies are reserved for frequent or disabling attacks
reference.pathophysiology: Benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood is regarded as part of the migraine spectrum and a migraine precursor. Attacks are thought to arise from transient dysfunction of central vestibular pathways, plausibly driven by the same paroxysmal neuronal excitability, channel dysfunction and brainstem/trigeminovascular mechanisms that underlie migraine. The strong association with a personal or family history of migraine, and the tendency to evolve into typical migraine, support a shared pathophysiology; a subset overlaps with the calcium-channel dysfunction seen in familial hemiplegic migraine.
additionalDifferentials: Epileptic seizures, particularly focal seizures with a vestibular or temporal aura
Peripheral labyrinthine disorders including vestibular neuritis and labyrinthitis
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo in older children
Posterior fossa tumour affecting the brainstem or cerebellum
Vestibular migraine in older children and adolescents
Benign paroxysmal torticollis of infancy and paroxysmal tonic upgaze
additionalInvestigations: Detailed history and eyewitness account or home video of the attacks
Neurological and otological examination performed between attacks
Audiometry and vestibular testing if there is hearing loss or persistent signs
EEG only if epileptic seizures are seriously suspected (usually normal)
MRI brain if there are atypical features, persistent nystagmus or posterior fossa signs
ECG to exclude a cardiac cause of episodic events where the history is atypical
redFlags: Persistent or interictal nystagmus, ataxia or other neurological signs suggesting a posterior fossa lesion
Hearing loss or tinnitus pointing to a peripheral or structural cause
Headache with early-morning vomiting, papilloedema or increasing head circumference
Progressive or worsening attacks, or a new focal neurological deficit
Altered consciousness during episodes, which points towards seizures
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent; it is a benign, self-limiting condition that resolves spontaneously over months to a few years. Many children subsequently develop migraine in later childhood or adolescence.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing attacks as epileptic seizures and starting antiepileptic drugs
Failing to recognise the strong link with migraine and the family history
Overlooking a posterior fossa tumour when interictal neurological signs are present
Ordering unnecessary investigations in a child with a typical, self-limiting picture
Confusing it with benign paroxysmal torticollis or other paroxysmal infantile syndromes
references: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3)
Swaiman's Pediatric Neurology: Principles and Practice
management: Reassure the family that this is a benign migraine-related syndrome that resolves spontaneously and needs no routine drug treatment
Manage attacks with reassurance and a safe environment during the brief episodes of vertigo and unsteadiness
Advise on migraine hygiene including regular sleep, hydration and trigger avoidance given the migraine association
Monitor for evolution into typical migraine in later childhood and treat accordingly if it develops
Undertake interval neurological and audiological examination to confirm normal findings between attacks
Investigate with brain MRI and further testing, and escalate, if nystagmus persists, posterior fossa signs appear or features are atypical
